_about: Manpower (the grand campaign). Every nation has a reserve of men fit to bear arms, counted in divisions' worth (15,000 men). The replacements that fill up worn corps and every new corps are drawn from it, and each month a class comes of age and joins it. A nation whose reserve is spent makes good only what the month's class allows and raises no new corps. The same rule holds for the player and the computer. The historical scenarios have none of this. Rules in src/campaign/manpower.ts.

notes.pool: The reserve a great power opens a campaign of September 1939 with, in divisions' worth. 'minor': any other country has 'pool' and 'perDiv' for each division it has under arms as the campaign opens.
notes.class: The class that comes of age each month with the whole homeland held, in divisions' worth; a minor's is 'classShare' of its reserve. It shrinks with the share of the homeland lost, counted by the worth of the provinces, but never under 'classFloor' of it. The reserve never holds more than 'most' times what it opened with.
notes.later: A campaign that opens after 1939 finds 'spentAYear' of each warring nation's reserve gone for every year of war behind it, to 'spentMost'.
notes.warn: The player is told when his reserve falls under these shares of what it opened with, and when it is spent.
notes.early: A say over the call-up. A country at war may call the next class up early: 'months' of classes join the reserve at once, and no class comes of age for the next 'gap' months, because the boys who would have are already with the colours: the same men, sooner. Where the reserve has room for fewer than 'months' of classes, only those come and the months without a class are fewer in step. A country with a standing call-up (east.json, mobilisation) may also hold it: no new corps are raised from the reserve while it is held, the waves wait, and the men of each wave that was not raised go to the corps in the field as drafts, over and above what the depots send and at no cost to the treasury. Only the player uses either.
